ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *kelh₂-der. Proto-Indo-European *kelh₂tís Proto-Germanic *hildiz Old Norse hildr Old Norse Gunnhildrder. Middle English gunne English gun From Middle English gunne, gonne, possibly from Gunnhild, a female given name formerly used as a nickname for engines of war (compare Nordic Gunn, a female name meaning “battle”). The name is composed of the Norse elements gunnr and hildr, both meaning "battle".
Related to ganef.

senses.d: A device for shooting projectiles or ditto (a shooter), functioning through stored energy: a firearm, cannon, harpoon gun/spear gun, raygun, etc, not a bow and arrow, or slingshot.
ex: Guns were considered improvements of crossbows and catapults.
Looking for wild meat to fill his family's freezer for the winter, the young man quietly raised his gun at the approaching deer.

senses.d: A very portable, short firearm, for hand use, which fires bullets or projectiles, such as a handgun, revolver, pistol, or Derringer.
A less portable, long firearm that fires bullets or projectiles; a rifle, either manual, automatic or semi-automatic; a flintlock, musket or shotgun.
A cannon with relatively long barrel, operating with relatively low angle of fire, and having a high muzzle velocity.
A cannon with a 6-inch/155mm minimum nominal bore diameter and tube length 30 calibers or more.
A firearm or cannon used for saluting or signalling.
ex: 21-gun salute

senses.d: Any implement designed to fire a projectile from a tube.
ex: air-pressure pellet gun
zipgun

senses.d: A device or tool that projects a substance.
ex: squirt gun
spray gun

senses.d: A device or tool that applies something rather than projecting it.
ex: a rivet gun
screw gun

senses.d: A long surfboard designed for surfing big waves (not the same as a longboard, a gun has a pointed nose and is generally a little narrower).
ex:
2000, Drew Kampion, surfline.com
by the winter of 1962, the Brewer Surfboards Hawaii gun was the most in-demand big-wave equipment on the North Shore.

senses.d: To shoot with a gun.
To cause to speed up.
ex: He gunned the engine.

senses.d: To offer vigorous support to (a person or cause).
ex: We're all gunning for you.

senses.d: To strongly desire or seek, and make a great effort to obtain (something which one is 'gunning for' or 'gunning to do').
To seek to attack someone; to take aim at someone; used with for.
ex: He's been gunning for you ever since you embarrassed him at the party.

senses.d: To practice fowling or hunting small game; chiefly in participial form: to go gunning.
Synonym of gun down (“to masturbate while making sustained eye contact with someone — typically a female prison officer — as a form of intimidation”).
ex: […] all inmates participated in such conduct, and […] "the inmates gunned only female staff, not the all-male security staff," he said.

senses.d: A magsman or street thief.

ety.text: Probably borrowed from flinke, flingge, Bavarian variant of German Flinte.
From pistole + -et. Ultimately from Czech píšťala (“whistle”).

Borrowed from German Pistole, from Czech píšťala (“firearm”, literally “tube, pipe”).

Probably from French pistole, ultimately from Czech píšťala (“firearm”, literally “tube, pipe”), from pištěti (“to whistle”), of imitative origin. Perhaps, however, from Italian pistolese (“from Pistoia (a city in Tuscany)”).
From Old French fuisil, foisil, from Vulgar Latin *focīlis (petra), from Latin focus. Compare Italian fucile.
From Vulgar Latin *focīlis [petra], derived from Latin focus. Compare French fusil, Friulian fusîl, Piedmontese fusil.
Italian scoppiettobor. Spanish escopeta Borrowed from Italian scoppietto.
Frankish *rīffilōnbor. Old French riflerbor. Middle English riflen English riflebor. Spanish rifle Borrowed from English rifle.
Borrowed from French fusil.
From French fusil, from Vulgar Latin petra (“stone”) + focilis (“of fire”) (flintstone), from focus (“fire”), from Latin focus (“fireplace, hearth”). Cognate of English fusillade.
Borrowed from English rifle, from Middle English, from Old French rifler (“to scrape off, plunder”), from Old Low Franconian Old Dutch *rifillon, frequentative of Proto-Germanic *rīfaną.
Inherited from Old French canon, corresponding to Italian cannone (from which borrowed most of the weaponry senses).

Akkadian 𒂵𒉡𒌑𒌝 (qanûm)bor. Ancient Greek κᾰ́ννᾰ (kắnnă)bor. Latin canna Italian cann(a) Proto-Indo-European *-ōder. Proto-Indo-European *-Hōder.? Latin -ōnem Italian -one Italian cannone From cann(a) (“cane, tube, pipe”) + -one (augmentative suffix).
From caño (“tube, pipe”) + -ón (augmentative).

From Italian cannone (“cannon”), from Latin canna (“reed, cane”), from Ancient Greek κάννα (kánna, “reed”), from Akkadian 𒄀 (qanû, “reed”), from Sumerian 𒄀𒈾 (gi.na). Or from Spanish cañón (“cannon”) (compare cânion).
Borrowed from German Haubitze.
Borrowed from French obus (“shell”).

From French obus (“shell”), from German Haubitze (“howitzer”), from Czech houfnice (“catapult”), from houf (“throng”), from Old High German houf (“heap”), from Proto-West Germanic *haup, from Proto-Germanic *haupaz.

es:disparar.gl: to shoot, to fire (e.g. a weapon, a rocket)

ety.text: Latinizing alteration of Old Spanish desparar, from Latin disparāre (“separate”), from dis- + parō (“make equal”), although it was taken as the negative of parō (“prepare, arrange”) in Romance.

pt:acelerar.gl: to accelerate (to increase speed or acquire speed, become swift)

chain.g: to quicken, hasten, speed up, accelerate

From gun + shot.

senses.d: The discharging a firearm.
ex: No gunshot wounds, Barricune observed, but marks of kicks, and couple that must have been made with a quirt.

senses.d: The firing of guns; gunfire.
ex: they heard gunshot all around them
the sound of distant gunshot

senses.d: The distance to which shot can be thrown from a gun; the reach or range of a gun.
ex: For those, who are come over to the royal party, are consequently supposed to be out of gunshot.

senses.d: A bullet, projectile, or other shot fired from a gun.

ety.text: From fucilare (“to shoot”) + -ata.
See scoppio (“explosion”), of onomatopoeic origin. Alternatively from Latin stloppus (“sound of a slap”).

senses.d: Shots from a gun or guns, typically creating loud report.
ex: Let's hide in the trees to avoid the gunfire.
Sergeant, direct your gunfire toward that copse of trees.

senses.d: The use of gunpowder-type weapons, mainly cannon, as opposed to swords or bayonets.
ex: Killing people became much easier and faster once armies started using gunfire.

senses.d: The time of firing of the morning gun or the evening gun.
Tea, a cup of tea, especially one served early in the morning before first parade.
ex: They had only in them the rolled mattresses, the neatly piled bed-boards and the empty tea-buckets of the orderly-men, empied of their last gun-fire.
